stories.headline: Tyler Boebert sentenced to 20 days in jail for probation violation in identity theft case
stories.summary:
A Garfield County judge sentenced Tyler Boebert, 21-year-old son of U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert, to 20 days in jail Thursday after he violated the terms of his probation stemming from a 2024 credit card and identity theft case. Tyler Boebert had originally pleaded guilty to attempted identity theft — a felony — after investigators linked him to a string of car break-ins and stolen credit card use in Rifle, and received a deferred sentence with two years of supervised probation.

His probation was revoked after he was arrested in Weld County in 2025 on a misdemeanor child abuse charge, to which he also pleaded guilty. A separate judge sentenced him to 20 days on that count, and Judge Elise Myer ordered Thursday that both sentences run concurrently, likely through a work release program.

Tyler Boebert still faces a separate Garfield County charge of child sexual exploitation related to an explicit video allegedly filmed with a 17-year-old girl when he was 18; Judge Myer noted those charges did not factor into Thursday's sentencing because he is presumed innocent. Rep. Lauren Boebert addressed the court on her son's behalf, asking for mercy while acknowledging he had not done everything right.

Myer declined to send Tyler Boebert to community corrections as prosecutors requested, noting he will carry a felony conviction as a consequence of his actions. She urged him to confront his struggles directly and accept available help.

stories.headline: Children's Hospital Colorado contempt trial opens over gender-affirming care for transgender youth
stories.summary:
A Denver judge took the rare step of closing her courtroom to the public Thursday as doctors from Children's Hospital Colorado testified anonymously about their decisions to stop writing prescriptions for young transgender patients. The doctors sought anonymity citing fear of federal government retaliation; Children's Hospital disclosed during the hearing that it has been referred again for federal investigation over its care of transgender youth.

Attorneys for the young patients are seeking to hold the hospital in contempt of a Colorado Supreme Court injunction that prohibits the hospital from refusing gender-affirming care, including hormone therapy and puberty-blockers. The potential penalty is $50,000 per day. The hospital has continued providing mental health support and lab testing but has not resumed writing prescriptions, meaning some patients may be entering puberty inconsistent with their gender identity or involuntarily detransitioning.

Attorneys for the patients argued that seven months after the lawsuit was filed and three months after the injunction was issued, nothing has materially changed for the affected children. One mother testified her daughter was forced to seek treatment out of state, while another said the family stopped seeing their Children's Hospital doctor altogether.

Children's legal team described the federal investigation as part of "a reign of terror by the federal government against transgender care providers." The contempt trial is expected to continue in coming days.

stories.headline: Denver metro home sales plunge 19% in August as prices hold flat and listings stall
stories.summary:
Closed home sales in the 11-county Denver metro area fell to 3,068 in August, a drop of 19% from July and 17% from a year earlier, according to the Denver Metro Association of Realtors' August Market Trends Report. Total sales volume declined 19% month over month to $2.2 billion, while the median close price edged down just 1.7% from July to $594,495 — essentially flat compared to August 2025.

Homes sat on the market longer, with the median days on market jumping 29% from July to 27 days, though still faster than last August's 30-day median. Active listings remained nearly unchanged at 13,080, while pending sales — a leading indicator of demand — rose 2.4% to 3,332, suggesting some residual buyer interest even as new listings fell 10%.

A widening gap between detached single-family homes and attached properties such as condos and townhomes continued to define the market. Detached inventory fell 4.2% year over year while attached inventory grew 9.9%; attached homes sat on the market a median of 45 days compared to 24 days for detached, and attached prices dropped nearly 4.9% compared to flat detached prices.

DMAR Market Trends Committee chair Amanda Snitker described August as resisting easy summary, citing falling sales, flat prices and stretched timelines occurring simultaneously. She attributed the unsettled conditions to broader economic uncertainty including unresolved inflation, shifting tariff policy and an uncommitted Federal Reserve.

stories.headline: Colorado Community College System seeks developer for 145-acre Lowry Campus redevelopment
stories.summary:
The Colorado Community College System on Thursday launched a formal search for a developer to redevelop the Lowry Campus, a 145-acre property straddling the Denver-Aurora border along the Quebec Street corridor. Approximately 136 acres will become available by the end of 2028, when CCCS operations are relocated or consolidated onto the remaining nine acres; the site includes 18 buildings totaling about 566,000 square feet, some of which may be candidates for adaptive reuse.

CCCS issued a request for proposals through BidNet Direct with submissions due November 16. JLL is serving as the system's real estate adviser and described the opportunity as combining "scale, location and market fundamentals that are increasingly rare in established urban markets." The surrounding area has seen 28.1% population growth since 2010.

The developer will bear responsibility for infrastructure improvements including utility connections and road reconstruction; the site's water, wastewater and stormwater systems date to the 1940s and will require upgrades. Public financing tools including Tax Increment Financing and metro districts may be used to offset those costs.

The Lowry Campus is situated near the Fitzsimons Medical Campus, Stanley Marketplace, parks and public transit. CCCS Chancellor Marielena DeSanctis called the property "an incredible asset for the Aurora and Denver communities" and said it will enrich surrounding neighborhoods.

stories.headline: Nuggets officially sign DeMar DeRozan; team also announces return to Boulder
stories.summary:
The Denver Nuggets have officially signed veteran guard DeMar DeRozan, a six-time NBA All-Star, after the two sides had reached an agreement last month. DeRozan joins a Nuggets core built around three-time MVP Nikola Jokic, Jamal Murray and Aaron Gordon as the team prepares for the upcoming season.

Analysis surrounding the signing has focused on whether DeRozan will slot into the starting lineup or serve as a Sixth Man of the Year candidate, given his offensive skill set and veteran experience. Jokic was reported to have been involved in recruiting DeRozan, a move some observers have interpreted as a signal from the superstar about the direction he wants the roster to take.

Separately, the Nuggets announced that the team will return to Boulder, though details on the nature of that visit were not immediately specified. Jokic also drew attention this week for candid remarks about his growing discomfort with NBA fame and his desire to return to the quiet lifestyle he had before becoming a global star.

stories.headline: University of Denver hockey unveils championship rings for record 11th national title
stories.summary:
The University of Denver men's hockey program unveiled its national championship rings Friday, commemorating the program's NCAA-record 11th title won at the 2026 Frozen Four in Las Vegas. The Pioneers defeated the Wisconsin Badgers 2-1 in an improbable comeback on April 11, delivering the program's third national championship in five years. Players, coaches and staff received their rings at a private ceremony Thursday night.

The rings are heavily themed around the number 11 and the Las Vegas setting, featuring the phrase "National C11ampions" and a removable poker chip engraved with the team's records — 13-11-2 and 29-11-3 — representing the 16-0-1 run DU went on to close the season. Head coach David Carle led the Pioneers through that stretch.

Denver begins its quest for a 12th title with a road trip to Alaska-Anchorage on October 2-3, followed by three consecutive home weekends at Magness Arena against the USA Hockey National Team Development Program, Michigan and Boston College.

stories.headline: CU Buffaloes shift preparation to Weber State after season-opening win at Georgia Tech
stories.summary:
The Colorado Buffaloes football program has turned its attention to Saturday's home game against Weber State following a season-opening road victory at Georgia Tech. The game will be broadcast with Peter Sousa handling play-by-play and Leger Douzable as color analyst, while the Buffs' own broadcast will feature Mark Johnson, Gary Barnett and sideline reporter Andy Lindahl.

The win at Georgia Tech provided an early confidence boost for the program heading into a full schedule. Weber State represents a mid-major opponent that Colorado will be expected to handle at home before conference play intensifies.

stories.headline: RTD bus shuttles to replace A Line service to Denver airport this weekend for maintenance
stories.summary:
Travelers heading to Denver International Airport this weekend should expect bus shuttles in place of Regional Transportation District A Line train service during scheduled maintenance windows. On Saturday, shuttles will replace the A Line between the Peoria and Denver Airport stations from 3 a.m. to 3 p.m., while Sunday's maintenance will affect the segment between Union Station and the Central Park station from 5:30 a.m. to 11:30 a.m.

RTD urged customers to allow additional travel time when connecting to and from the airport during the maintenance periods. The A Line will continue to operate normally outside those affected segments during the respective windows. Information on shuttle boarding locations is available on the RTD website.

stories.headline: 25 years on, World Trade Center steel stands as memorial across Colorado and beyond
stories.summary:
On the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, roughly a dozen pieces of structural steel from the destroyed World Trade Center towers are on display at memorial sites throughout Colorado, including at fire stations in Louisville and Denver and at locations in Colorado Springs, Grand Junction, Broomfield and Pueblo. The history and fate of that steel is chronicled in a newly released book, "Scattered Steel," by Boulder-raised brothers Max and Sam Holleran, who trace how nearly 2,000 pieces of WTC steel were distributed to all 50 states and to overseas sites as far away as New Zealand, Italy and Canada.

"The agony of the steel — the twisting — is a metaphor for the people who died that day," Max Holleran told The Denver Post. "Bringing this steel to all parts of the country gives communities closure — a kind of burial." With few traditional burials possible after the attacks killed nearly 3,000 people, communities turned to the steel as a means of physical mourning and remembrance.

In Colorado Springs, 84-year-old Don Addy, former president of the National Homeland Defense Foundation, was responsible for bringing a half-dozen pieces of WTC steel to the city's military bases. Standing beneath a large mangled I-beam at Fort Carson's Gate 1 this week, Addy reflected on the countless 9/11 ceremonies he has attended over the past quarter century.

The authors argue that the steel served as "proxy funerals" for a tragedy in which traditional burial rites were largely impossible, giving communities across the country a tangible point of connection to the day's victims.

stories.headline: Bomb threat at Silverthorne hotel prompts evacuations; no credible threat found
stories.summary:
A bomb threat at The Block Hotel & Commons in Silverthorne on Friday afternoon prompted evacuations of the hotel, the adjacent River's Edge Condominiums and the Summit Blue subdivision, along with a shelter-in-place order for nearby residents. Silverthorne officials issued an alert about the active threat at 2:18 p.m.

Bomb squads from the Jefferson County and Eagle County sheriff's offices responded and cleared the building at 491 Rainbow Drive. The shelter-in-place order was lifted at 4:25 p.m., and officials subsequently announced that "no credible threat was found in the building and there is no threat to the public."

stories.headline: Judge dismisses Telluride ski area owner's lawsuit against local officials over failed resort sale
stories.summary:
A San Miguel County district judge has dismissed with prejudice a lawsuit filed by Telluride ski area owner Chuck Horning against three former local officials who orchestrated an unsuccessful plan to purchase the resort. Judge Laura E. H. Harvell ruled that Horning's claims against former Mountain Village Mayor Marti Prohaska, former Telluride Mayor Pro Tem Meehan Fee and former Mountain Village town manager Paul Wisor "fail to state a plausible claim" and are "deficient."

Horning had sued the three leaders alleging they used their positions to coerce him into selling 51% of the ski area by promising to help end a ski patrol strike that shut down the resort for 10 days over the New Year's holiday last season. Investigations by both Telluride and Mountain Village previously found no laws were broken. The closure devastated the local tourism economy: net taxable sales in Telluride fell 11% and Mountain Village spending dropped 19.5% during the 2025-26 ski season.

Prohaska said the ruling's "resounding rejection" revealed Horning's claims as baseless, adding that he was presented with an opportunity to model a new paradigm for the ski industry but instead chose to "distort the intent into a made-up story." Because the dismissal is with prejudice, Horning cannot refile the lawsuit. The long-running tensions between Horning and the two mountain towns — involving gondola funding, water rates and resort investment levels — predated the strike by several years.

topStory.headline: US-Canada Trade War Strains Border Communities as Canadians Shift Buying Habits and Retaliatory Tariffs Take Hold
topStory.summary:
The escalating trade dispute between the United States and Canada is reshaping daily life in border communities and driving a broad shift in Canadian consumer behavior, as residents increasingly avoid American goods in response to tariffs and inflammatory rhetoric from President Donald Trump. Canada's retaliatory tariffs, ranging from 15 to 50 percent on roughly $20 billion worth of U.S. imports including steel, aluminum, dairy, appliances and clothing, took effect this week, answering a new round of U.S. tariffs that went into force on August 22 targeting nearly $20 billion in Canadian products.

The tension is felt acutely in the twin border towns of Fort Frances, Ontario, and International Falls, Minnesota, where residents share family ties, social networks and a long history of cross-border commerce. Fort Frances Mayor Andrew Hallikas said Canadians are "irate" at Trump over his tariff policies and his repeated suggestions that Canada should become the 51st U.S. state, calling that prospect flatly impossible. "You cannot imagine how angry that makes us," Hallikas said. "We will never become the 51st state." American business owners in International Falls have reported declining sales from Canadian customers, while both communities wait uncertainly for the trade dispute to resolve.

Beyond the border towns, a broader nationalist shopping movement has taken hold across Canada. Market research firm Narrative Research, which has tracked Canadian attitudes for roughly 18 months, says the drive to buy Canadian is "not a fleeting sentiment" and is expected to last. In Toronto grocery stores, red maple leaf labels now mark domestically produced goods, and shoppers say they are actively switching brands to avoid American products.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney accused the United States of inserting last-minute demands into trade negotiations — terms he described as "uneconomic, unfair" and damaging to Canada's interests — before talks collapsed ahead of the latest round of U.S. tariffs. Economists at advisory firm Oxford Economics note that direct price impacts on consumers remain modest for now, given that targeted goods represent a small share of the average consumer basket, but warn that a prolonged or deepened trade war could bring rising prices and job losses. Both nations have signaled they remain at an impasse, with no clear timeline for resolution.
